doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: New Orleans jazz, Armstrong and the Texas lawyer
summary: Few listen to New Orleans music now; Armstrong's genius changed a Texas civil-rights lawyer.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Years ago I went, it might have been the same jazz educators’ gathering that you were at. There was a panel about, that was entitled “Trad Jazz Is Alive and Well” and it had some record label people and some players. But on the program for the three or four days there was no trad jazz groups that performed. I started thinking about jazz in the larger sense has been elevated to a high art form and it’s in the universities and it is studied and you can get Ph.D.s in it but is New Orleans music and trad jazz and those twenty or thirty years, do you feel that that is respected as much as the music from John Coltrane and forward?

I don’t think a lot of people listen to New Orleans music anymore. It’s too bad because it’s still great music. There was a lot of brilliance in the 1920s and coming forward. And it still speaks, at least to me today. Louis Armstrong for example, was a voice for the © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

ages. I mean I don’t think he will ever be obsolete. But still I think most people know Louis from the singing he did say during the 1950s to the end of his life than they do from the times when he was breaking through and establishing himself as the future of music. And there was one — Charles — what is his name — one of the great white Civil Rights lawyers had written about how he grew up in Texas in a world of segregation and had assumed all of the things that go with segregation and Jim Crow about inferiority/superiority, and then you heard Louis Armstrong play and you said this man is a genius. And he had to face the fact that if he’s a genius then all these other stuff can’t be true. So it’s amazing how music can change so much in a person. But at any rate I think that the great music is still alive but a capacity to hear certain great music isn’t always there. I mean I think that you know I think that people who listen to classical music, a lot of them really can’t abide things like motets or early masses, and that’s still great music. So yes, I think for me the masterpieces remain masterpieces and you can listen to them at any time.
